confidence_why: 3 independent first-hand descriptions agree (2 state the same rule, 0 refine it); none contradicts.
catalog_quote: (11) Word Stress — Stress the initial syllable of a word. This rule is inviolable.
sweep_summary: Bengali (beng1280) is in the catalog as fixed-strict initial (Hayes & Lahiri 1991:55). this search of works with stress in the title had one item, Khan's 2008 UCLA dissertation on Bengali intonation; an open author copy was found on his Reed College page and downloaded (the PDF text is garbled, so section 6 'Stress', pp. 20-34, was scanned at 250 dpi). Khan reviews all prior stress work and concludes that primary stress is initial, non-contrastive and phonetically weak but phonologically salient (lax/nasal vowel distribution, loanword truncation, syncope, metathesis, enclitic alternations, pitch accent attraction), with frequent secondary stress on later odd syllables; he notes two minority weight-sensitive analyses (Shaw 1984 second-syllable stress unless the first is closed; Das 2001 for Tripura Bengali) and a loanword exception for some speakers (fn. 11). This confirms the catalog's classification and does not supersede Hayes & Lahiri 1991, which remains the deciding statement; Khan 2008 is a strong corroborating source and supplies the literature map. Two further open copies were found and read on the same page: Khan 2010 JIPA illustration (p. 223: 'consistently word-initial') and Khan 2014 Prosodic Typology II chapter (p. 84 + fn. 3), the latter previously recorded as paywalled in REF_UNIVERSE. nothing remains unread.

new_statements.quote: Although stress in Bengali appears to be phonetically weak, it is nevertheless phonologically salient. Bengali clearly does assign a special status to particular syllables, whose properties are roughly equivalent to the non-phonetic correlates of stress in English. This special status is always a property of the initial syllable of native monomorphemic words, and normally also on borrowings and complex words. There is often a similar status on all odd-numbered syllables after the initial syllable. [fn. 11:] Primary stress is nearly always word-initial; however, some words borrowed from Perso-Arabic, English, or Sanskrit can bear non-initial primary stress in some speakers' pronunciations.
new_statements.citation: Khan, Sameer ud Dowla. 2008. Intonational phonology and focus prosody of Bengali. Ph.D. dissertation, UCLA.
new_statements.locator: sec. 6.4, p. 25 (p. 60), with fn. 11; cf. sec. 6.6 summary p. 33 (p. 68)
new_statements.reading: Primary word stress is fixed on the initial syllable (with optional secondary stresses on later odd-numbered syllables); it is non-contrastive and phonetically weak but phonologically real, shown by vowel-quality/nasality restrictions, syncope, metathesis, enclitic hiatus and pitch accent attraction. The only qualifications are speaker-variable non-initial stress in some Perso-Arabic/English/Sanskrit loans (fn. 11) and two minority weight-sensitive analyses (Shaw 1984; Das 2001 for Tripura Bengali) that Khan reports but does not adopt. This confirms the catalog's fixed-strict initial coding and its word domain; it refines the picture by documenting secondary stress and the loanword exception.

sources.quote: In this form of Bengali, the stress is dominantly initial; and word-stress surrenders itself entirely to sentence stress, the initial syllable of the first important word in a sense-group having the stress, and the other words losing their stress if they possess it when isolated. Learned Sanskrit words not fully naturalised, however, frequently retain a non-initial stress, which is generally on the first long syllable or closed syllable from the end. (S. K. Chatterji, 'Bengali Phonetics,' op. cit., § 58.) The main point of difference between pan-IA. accent and the Bengali Standard Dialect accent therefore consists in this: Bengali accent is initial, and a Bengali phrase, or breath-group, or sense-group, has only one stress, an initial one.

sources.quote: The dominant audible quality in Bengali (as in French) is not, as in most European and Indo-Aryan languages, a fixed verbal accent, whether of force or duration, but a phrasal accent of duration. In French, the voice dwells longer on a final or penultimate syllable before a pause (or, in verse, a caesura). In Bengali an initial syllable is thus prolonged, and the syllable thus dwelt on comes immediately after a pause (or, in verse, a caesura or jphak). It is the regular recurrence of these prolonged syllables which constitutes the rhythm of metre.
sources.locator: § IX 'Phrasal Accent', printed p. 11; continued printed p. 12
sources.note: Anderson's system statement: no fixed word-level accent; the prominence is an initial PHRASAL accent of duration (prolongation of the syllable immediately after a pause or caesura), which is the basis of metre. sources.quote: English and Bengali have different rules for stress placement. In English, stress can fall on any syllable of the word (Beckman, 2012). In Bengali, stress is always on the first syllable of a word (Khan, 2008). Therefore, it implies that Bengali is more regular in stressed-interval duration and can have transfer on the English produced by Bengali speakers.
sources.note: marginal: Durational rhythm metrics for Bengali L1 vs Bengali-accented English; characterises Bengali as syllable-timed, no word-stress analysis.
